abstract: Ramp AI Index for October 2026, published November 11, 2026 by Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian under the title 'New Fronts in the AI Trade'. The index tracks AI adoption and spend among more than 85,000 US businesses on Ramp's corporate card and bill-pay platform, which makes it a payment-based rather than self-reported measure of firm AI use. Where the preceding 'Cracks in the AI Thesis' series argued that growth assumptions were breaking down, this edition holds those risks in place and looks for where new growth is coming from: use cases beyond coding, and a three-way vendor race. It introduces a department-level AI spend dataset for the first time.
keyFindings: Overall AI adoption among Ramp businesses reached 56.8 percent in October 2026, up 1 percentage point, slightly faster than September's 0.66-point gain - which is itself a restatement of the 0.62 points published one edition earlier.
Anthropic rose 1.1 points to 44.8 percent of businesses while OpenAI held flat at 40.6 percent, so OpenAI's September catch-up did not continue.
SpaceXAI (the post's name for the vendor the dashboard table still lists as xAI) led breakout growth, reaching 6.3 percent of Ramp businesses, up 2.2 points in a month.

Spend intensity rose at the top: the top 1 percent of firms now spend a median $10.2K per employee per month, up 9 percent, against $801 for the top 10 percent (roughly flat) and $16.32 for the median firm, up $0.93.

Concentration is extreme and unchanged: 1 percent of businesses drive 80 percent of the revenues to OpenAI and Anthropic, and that top 1 percent is largely VC-backed firms in tech, finance and technical services.

New department-level data: engineering teams drove 72 percent of all classified AI spend in October, down from highs earlier in the summer, while customer success and support operations reached 13.3 percent of classified spend, up from 0.8 percent in June.

Executive leadership teams also grew modestly, but Kharazian notes customer-service spend has not reached the hypergrowth engineering showed early in 2026, and that these use cases favour cheaper, faster models over the highest-margin frontier ones.
Frontier models took 69.5 percent of spend in October, up from 67.7 percent.
Prices keep falling: the average price per million tokens fell 21 percent over the last month, and token volume growth continues to outpace token spend.
Total AI spend rose 1.65 percent from September to a new peak; October token spend grew 2.1 percent month over month for OpenAI and 0.5 percent for Anthropic.
methodology: Aggregated corporate card and bill-pay transaction data from more than 85,000 US businesses on Ramp, reported monthly as vendor-level adoption shares and per-employee spend cohorts. Adoption is defined as paying for a vendor's subscriptions or tokens in the month. Firms are assigned to NAICS sectors and size segments by internal models over internal and third-party data on revenue and headcount. The department-level series introduced in this edition is a share of classified spend, not of all spend, so unclassified spend is excluded from the denominator and the shares are not shares of a firm's total AI budget. The top-1 percent spend cohort is a small group and its estimate is volatile; Ramp has revised it across all prior periods before when vendors were added. The index is mirrored on FRED as RAMPAIALL and sibling series, which is the reliable staleness check for this series.
qualifiers: Not comparable with Census BTOS, which jobsdata.ai plots on ai-adoption-rate: BTOS asks a probability sample of about 1.2 million US businesses whether they used AI in any business function in the last two weeks, while this counts paid vendor subscriptions among Ramp's self-selected customer base, which skews toward startups and technology firms and reads more than twice as high. Carried as a directional overlay for that reason. The department-level customer-support share is carried as an overlay on customer-service-automation on the same logic: it measures where AI money is going, not the share of customer interactions handled without a human, which is what that graph plots, and a rise from 0.8 to 13.3 percent of classified spend in four months is a spend-mix shift off a very small base rather than a measured automation rate. Kharazian's own caveat on the headline adoption metric still holds: with more than half of businesses paying for AI and many paying several vendors, vendor share says less about adoption than it did in 2023.
